target_customer: Travelers seeking lodging and hosts monetizing spare space, two sided marketplace
problem: Travelers wanted cheaper and more local places to stay while homeowners had unused rooms with no trusted way to rent them. The founders started by renting air mattresses during a conference when hotels sold out.
business_model: Marketplace take rate on bookings from guests and hosts

founders.name: Brian Chesky
founders.background_notes: Listed on the YC page as Founder and CEO.

founders.name: Nathan Blecharczyk
founders.background_notes: Listed on the YC page as Founder and CTO.

founders.name: Joe Gebbia
founders.background_notes: Listed on the YC page as Founder and CPO.

competitors.name: Couchsurfing
competitors.what: Free hospitality exchange network founded in 2004, the main inspiration cited by the founders

competitors.name: Craigslist
competitors.what: Classifieds with listings for short term stays; Airbnb also posted its own listings there early on

competitors.name: Hostels.com
competitors.what: Hostel booking site described in one account as the closest competitor at the time

technical_complexity.rationale: A listing and booking website was standard web engineering; the hard parts were trust, payments, photography and scaling across countries, not research.

defensibility.rationale: Two sided supply and demand plus reviews created strong network effects, and the brand became the generic name for the category.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Vacation rental incumbents like HomeAway already listed 225,000 rentals by 2011 per Fortune, but none stopped Airbnb. It IPO'd in December 2020.

market_need_then: Hotel sell outs at big conferences and the 2008 recession pushed hosts to earn extra income and travelers to seek cheaper stays. Craigslist and Couchsurfing already showed demand for informal stays.

branding.name_origin: Started as AirBed and Breakfast, from the air mattresses the founders rented to three guests in 2007, then shortened to Airbnb in 2009 to drop the literal air mattress association.
branding.domain_note: Moved from airbedandbreakfast.com to airbnb.com in 2009, per a namefi article.

identity.logo: Bélo, a coral symbol introduced in July 2014 replacing a blue bubble wordmark, designed by London agency DesignStudio
identity.visual_style: Coral red with clean sans serif type after 2014

branding.brand_signature: The Bélo symbol and the belonging message, introduced in 2014

rebrands.why: Shortened to be memorable and drop the air mattress association
Define belonging as the core idea; the logo was widely mocked at launch

branding.community_and_virality: The 2014 logo was mocked widely online and the brand later recovered per Creative Bloq. Early cereal box promotions during 2008 kept the company alive but specifics were not confirmed by sources.

brand_strength.rationale: Airbnb became a category defining name worldwide, with a distinct logo, strong press about its rebrand and a hosting community; the brand supported growth to a 100 billion dollar first day market value.

pivots.from: AirBed and Breakfast, air mattresses at conferences
pivots.to: Broad lodging marketplace under the Airbnb name
pivots.why: Name and offering broadened beyond air mattresses to any space

outcome_analysis: Airbnb grew from a 2008 air mattress rental into a global marketplace after the Winter 2009 YC batch, raising a Sequoia seed, a Greylock and Sequoia Series A and a roughly 112 million dollar Series B from Andreessen Horowitz in 2011. Bookings fell almost 80 percent in the pandemic and it cut about a quarter of staff in May 2020, yet it listed on Nasdaq in December 2020 at a 47 billion dollar valuation and closed the first day near 100 billion.
notes: Seed figures differ: 585,000 dollars from Sequoia plus 30,000 from Youniversity per Wikipedia timeline versus 600,000 from Sequoia per Motley Fool. Series B reported as 112 million or about 114.9 million dollars; valuation commonly 1.3 billion, The Information says past 1 billion. Dates for Series A and Series B only have a year. Wimdu, Roomorama and 9flats appear only as later entrants, so they are excluded from the 2009 list. The cereal box promotion names were not found. Founder employers, education and ages were not sourced. IPO proceeds given as 3.5 billion dollars; others say 3.7 billion.
